interpretation: Pre-existing mixed-species meter marks are more likely than Thalassia-only meter marks to remain seagrass-occupied after exact-point Thalassia loss, and most target alternative occupancy retains at least one species already present before focal loss. This supports a community-insurance pattern based primarily on persistence of pre-existing community members rather than only post-loss colonization.
next_hypothesis: Test whether retaining another seagrass in the loss year predicts higher one-year Thalassia return at the same meter mark than becoming seagrass-bare, using a separately frozen three-year exact-point transition.
claim_boundary: The source-mixture association is consistent with ecological insurance but does not prove facilitation; mixed patches may share persistent habitat quality.
Retention of another seagrass preserves occupancy but does not imply equivalent habitat function or ecosystem services.
Species appearing after focal loss are observational appearances, not proven colonization or competitive replacement.
Do not generalize the pooled Tampa effect into a Lower-Tampa-specific effect without an independently estimable test.
